name: Glacial-Litany
geological_features: Continental ice sheets with embedded debris layers
specific_features: Ice algae that bloom in geometric patterns visible from orbit
Wind-carved ice formations that produce mournful tonal sounds
description: Glacial-Litany is a large ice world with a breathable atmosphere cold enough to freeze exposed skin in minutes. Continental ice sheets cover eighty percent of the surface, their blue-white expanse broken by fjord systems where subglacial volcanic activity keeps narrow channels of water liquid year-round. The remaining twenty percent consists of permafrost tundra where hardy flora clings to existence in the brief seasonal warming periods that bring temperatures just above the threshold for photosynthesis.

Wind is the constant companion on Glacial-Litany, howling across the ice sheets at speeds that would flatten unsheltered structures. The wind carves the ice into towering formations that act as natural wind instruments, producing deep, resonant tones that shift and harmonize as conditions change. Inhabitants describe the sound as a litany, a continuous chanting that rises and falls with the storms, giving the planet its name and an atmosphere of solemn, ceaseless prayer.

The ice algae of Glacial-Litany are unique in the known galaxy, photosynthetic organisms that bloom in precise geometric patterns driven by the crystal structure of the ice they inhabit. From orbit, these blooms create vast mandalas of green and gold across the ice sheets, patterns so regular they were initially mistaken for artificial constructions. The algae are the foundation of the planet's biosphere, supporting a food chain that extends through the fjord ecosystems to include fish-analogs and filter-feeding invertebrates of considerable size.

Natural gas hydrates locked in the permafrost represent an enormous energy reserve, but extraction threatens to destabilize the permafrost layer and accelerate a warming cycle that models predict would fundamentally alter the planet's ecology. The rare lichens that grow in the tundra zones produce compounds with remarkable antibiotic properties, supporting a small but lucrative pharmaceutical harvesting industry. Research stations along the fjords study the algae patterns for insights into biological self-organization, while the wind-carved ice continues its ancient litany overhead.
